Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger with a16z's Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller on the next wave of semiconductor innovation and the physical constraints shaping the AI buildout:

Drawing on his experience designing Intel's 386 and 486 processors, Pat explains how AI could transform chip design, but also why faster design alone won't solve the industry's biggest problems.

They examine the bottlenecks in manufacturing, memory bandwidth, advanced packaging, and power, and why today's explosion of specialized AI chips may eventually consolidate around a smaller number of architectures.

They also discuss the potential for new memory technologies, the shift from copper to optical networking, and why energy capacity could become a major constraint on AI growth.

Finally, they revisit Pat's VMware years to ask what virtualization might look like when infrastructure is built for agents rather than humans.

Ok, well I'm going to talk about a token that everyone knows but has been very much forgotten about, and I thought I would never ever write about.

The bull case for BAT (please stay with me): 

Brave is one of the few crypto native companies that won in the real world. $100M+ annualized revenue. 126M monthly users, 55M Daus. Its own search index doing 2.5B queries a month. 

People use it because it is fast and private performant browser, not because of a token anymore (although they did use the token to incentivise growth for a long time).

Its advertising business is very successful, alongside its paid search API. 

BAT trades at a $170M market cap. Fully circulating. No unlocks.

That is 1.7x revenue on a business growing users around 25% a year (not completely verified). And the $100M figure is from early 2025, 40M users ago. I can't find a more up to date figure. 

The token never captured any of that. That is why it went nowhere for five years. Roadmap 4.0 is the first real attempt to fix it.

TLDR on 4.0:

Unified Brave Wallet - Cards, self-custody crypto and Rewards in one interface, native in the browser.

BravePay - A private, self-custody stablecoin payments layer. 

Brave Rewards Card - Virtual and physical. Earn BAT on everyday spend. They already have 150k on the waitlist before launch.

Buybacks (Big change) - A share of net revenue from the wallet, card and BravePay buys BAT. Opportunistic buybacks on top, disclosed publicly.

Distribution is Brave's massive edge, as it is for all successful businesses. 

Every crypto neobank is fighting for its first million users. Brave starts with 55M people opening the product every day. The wallet is already installed. Acquisition cost is zero.

BAT printed an all-time low in August. It has doubled since and still sits 94% below its 2021 high. The rerate has barely got going. 

Every token has a bear case, so in this case Brave has equity. Token holders technically don't own the $100M. Buybacks come from the new product lines only, and the percentage is undisclosed.

Bought BAT is not burned. It funds user rewards, and some recipients will sell.

The card has no launch date yet I don't think.

So this rerating that I think is possible is not a claim on Brave’s revenue. It is a cheap option on Brave monetising 126M users through payments, with BAT as the reward and the buyback sink. At 1.7x revenue with a new structural bidder, I think that option is mispriced.

What is it worth? I don't know. The buyback percentage isn’t disclosed and the new products aren’t live.

BAT traded at a $420M market cap last December. Before Roadmap 4.0, before buybacks and 20M users ago. Getting back there is 2.4x.

Every $10M a year of buybacks is roughly 6% of today’s market cap. Brave does $100M+ in revenue before payments even launch.

I’m not underwriting a specific number. I’m underwriting that I think $170M is the wrong one. If I'm wrong and nothing happens then I think the risk is underperformance more than anything. 

The thing that I think is also interesting here is a bigger pattern: 

Old tokens attached to businesses that survived are reworking value capture. Brave is unique as it has an unrivalled sizeable user base it can monetise and finally return value to token holders. 

Also, fun fact is Brave's founder invented javascript and co founded Mozilla.  

DYOR, NFA.

One life, it's worth a shot etc.

What can you actually do with a tokenized stock right now?

Mostly hold it and trade it. Almost all of the products people actually use around stocks still live inside banks.

Structured notes are a good example. 

They're products that pay you a regular coupon as long as a stock doesn't fall too far, and banks issued roughly $538B of callable structured notes last year. 

However, there’s basically no real onchain version of that market.

@notesystems is trying to turn that desk into a protocol on Robinhood Chain.

The easiest way to understand it is that a structured note is basically matching two different needs.

• One side of users has stablecoins and wants yield.
• The other side already owns a stock and wants protection if it falls hard.

Normally, a bank sits between them. Note Systems replaces that middle layer with smart contracts.

The stablecoin side deposits USDG and earns a coupon while the stock stays above a set barrier. The stock holder pays those coupons and gets downside protection without selling.

Everything is locked upfront, so the note itself doesn’t have margin calls or liquidations.

The interesting part is each COUPON and SHIELD position is an ERC-1155 token, so it can be moved, used as collateral, or plugged into other apps.

They already have Credit through Morpho and Omni through LayerZero built around that idea.

The full protocol is still on testnet for now, with 5k+ users and 48 note series so far.

The points pre-season is live too, rewards grow with how much of the protocol you use, and they carry into mainnet, follow @notesystems for updates.

Robinhood Chain already brought stocks onchain. Now Note Systems is trying to bring the financial products built around those stocks onchain too.

Our MORTGAS index hit a record low in the early 2020s when mortgage rates got below 3% and prices at the pump briefly got below $2/gallon.  Those days are long gone.

Gas prices first spiked in early 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, then they trended lower for the next few years until they spiked again this year with the US invasion of Iran.

Mortgage rates went from 3% up to 7% during the Fed's massive tightening cycle to address runaway inflation in 2022.  They too had been trending lower over the past few years, but they've moved higher again this year since the Iran War began.

Combined, our MORTGAS index is actually at a new record high right now, eclipsing the peak seen back in October 2023.  Consumers are feeling the pain as we head into midterm elections less than a month away.

Good riddance to Firmus' failed $30B IPO and shame on the lead bankers (JPM, MS, BofA) who tried to dump this crap on public investors.

The failure hammered public data center stocks yesterday, but longer term, it's healthy for the sector that investors rejected this extractive structure:

>58% of shares freely tradable from day 1, with no lock-up restrictions, despite a capital-intensive business needing years of funding.
>Only ~46MW operational against 900MW+ contracted.
>Valuation nearly tripled in two months, to $30B equity; wildly overpriced vs public comps
>Founder and co-CEO previously served prison time for insider trading.
>Major 1.6GW development partnership with CDC fell apart during the bookbuild.
>Bankers reportedly stood to collect A$215M in fees and explored a 50% price cut before abandoning the deal.

Public shareholders shouldn't be expected to provide overpriced exit liquidity for insiders while underwriting nearly all the execution risk.

Established listed operators with access to capital markets, proven execution and funded development pipelines should take share from these less disciplined private competitors as capital becomes more discriminating.

Let this be a lesson to boards and investment bankers across the sector.

Good work to the market for pushing back on this 💩

Think it was solid print. Wasn't expecting a big stock move either way as long as there were no surprises on base rent or NOI. Sounds like the CY26 exit might be a touch lower than expected (by ~50MWs of deliveries), but should make up for it in C1H27 and with the 600MW they plan to put into service over the next 12 months (gets you to 850MWs by F2Q28, which is more than expected). They also expect to sign these two expansion leases (250MWs) by calendar year end (at materially higher pricing, >15%), which is later than they were initially communicating over the summer, but good to put firm commitment on it despite the midterm noise (wasn't expecting them to communicate timeline on them).  
- These guys have a lot of different large campus opportunities in non-TX regions (LA and ND sound very pro DC and business), so confident they can continue to lead. Important to remember that Macquarie will be owed a lot of shares as they will have claim on ~25% of the NOI on the deals they are involved in. Unclear if this partnership will expand when they run through the initial set amount, and worth noting that it is North America only (not Finland for now). Finland was a touch disappointing, given only 100MWs expected to be delivered in 2028 and the rest through 2030+, but sounds like little risk and opt out options through each stage of build and power securing. 
Stock looks cheap to me but sector needs a jolt of momentum and bond market to cooperate.
